lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Riverside Cinema | Box Office Attendant | Metro City, USA | Aug 2025 - Present
- Sold tickets and concessions during evening shifts and balanced the cash drawer at close.
- Trained 3 new attendants on the ticketing system and the refund policy.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Writes the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes date of birth and nationality, personal details readers are not meant to weigh.
items.because: They are not evidence of qualifications and can distract from relevant experience and skills.

items.says: Education should not lead a résumé with several years of relevant work experience.
items.because: Leading with education delays the stronger evidence of current fit in the work and projects.

items.says: Riverside Cinema should follow the analyst roles.
items.because: Its current prominence draws attention away from the more relevant analyst experience.

items.says: The Riverside Cinema entry should be shortened or removed.
items.because: The cinema role does not establish the candidate’s analyst career direction.

items.says: The opening bullet lists duties but gives no evidence of their outcome or quality.
items.because: A reader can picture the tasks but cannot tell what value or result the work delivered.

items.says: The training bullet should come before the duties bullet.
items.because: Training is the stronger contribution in the entry and would be easier to notice first.

items.says: The training result is missing.
The bullet names the training topics but not how the attendants were taught.
The dashboard bullet names the deliverable but not the analytical approach behind it.
“That” makes it unclear whether marketing used the dashboard or the customers.
The described left join cannot find customers with no orders by counting null customer names.
items.because: Starting with orders excludes customers with no orders; a null customer name instead indicates an unmatched order or a null name.

items.says: The bullet spends too much space on join details without saying what the finding enabled or changed.
items.because: The method detail overwhelms the finding and leaves the analysis’s business value unclear.

items.says: The campaign-attribution result is buried after three methods.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the business-relevant increase.

items.says: The reduction in ad hoc data requests has no comparison period.
The A/B test uses repeated unadjusted significance checks as an invalid stopping rule.
items.because: Stopping at the first ordinary p-value below 0.05 raises the false-positive rate above 5%.

items.says: The bullet gives no measured checkout result or decision from the test.
items.because: The threshold does not show which variant performed better, by how much, or whether the test informed a decision.

items.says: “Until significance” is vague and repeats the stated stopping rule.
The analysis bullet does not lead with its strongest result.
items.because: The staffing change and hold-time reduction are more compelling than the description of the analysis.

items.says: The bullet does not show how the analysis identified the evening peak.
The first-person pronoun does not fit résumé bullet style.
“Writes” uses present tense for work in a role that ended in July 2022.
The list of secondary duties buries the fraud extract’s 10-hour monthly saving.
items.because: The unrelated support duties distract from the analyst contribution and make it harder to see.

items.says: The bullet gives no technical or analytical detail about how the extract was automated.
The forecast bullet does not name the modeling approach.
items.because: The reader cannot see the technical approach behind the forecast.

items.says: The forecast’s percentage error metric does not explain its denominator.
items.because: Mean absolute error is usually read in the target’s units, so the percentage needs a denominator to be interpretable.

items.says: The change from 300 to 200 empty-station hours is a 33.3% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The reduction is 100 hours out of the original 300.

items.says: The empty-station result should lead the project bullets.
items.because: It is the project’s strongest measured result and would be easier to notice first.

items.says: The replay bullet does not say what rebalancing approach produced the change.
The change from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not a 15% increase.
items.because: Relative to the original 60% hit rate, the increase is 25%.

items.says: The bullet does not define what counts as a forecast hit.
items.because: Without a threshold or rule, the reader cannot judge the metric.

items.says: The unique-household result does not state the number of households identified.
items.because: The 9,000 logs show the amount of data handled, not the scale of the finding.

items.says: “After the project ended” adds timeline detail that weighs down the guide bullet.
